states.name: caret
states.gap: B buys its tightness at the cost of separation: only 5px (2.5 CSS px) of white sits between the 's' and the caret — barely more than one of B's own 4px stems — so at typing speed the bar can read as a stroke of the glyph rather than a mark beside it. Vertically B is also 2px shorter (74px vs 76px device; 37 vs 38 CSS px), leaving 19px of clearance to the next line's ascenders against A's 21px, and 18px of naked blue above the ascender line instead of A's 20px.
states.gapTheirs: The caret floats off the word: 8px device (4 CSS px) of white between the right edge of the 's' in 'steps' and the caret's left edge, vs 5px (2.5 CSS px) in B. Least-squares fit of the glyph grid (advance 25.9px) puts A's caret centre ~5.4px right of the character-cell boundary — ~21% of a cell of drift — vs ~1.9px (~7%) in B. Compounding it, A's body stems measure 3px against the same 6px caret, so the caret is 2.0x the stem weight vs B's 1.5x: a blunt bar parked in the space rather than a nib at the insertion point.
states.verdict: This is a near-tie decided by three pixels, and anyone claiming otherwise hasn't measured: same #00B5FF, same 6px width, same hard-edged pixel-snapped rendering, same full-line-box height, no selection shown in either. What separates them is that A's caret sits ~5px right of the character cell boundary — you finish typing 'steps' and the caret is out in the space, so for a beat you don't know whether the next letter lands before or after the gap. B's caret sits on the boundary and hugs the letterform, and at 1.5x the stem weight instead of 2.0x it belongs to the same hand that set the type. Neither trims the caret to text height, so both are still 1.8x fenceposts with 18-20px of dead blue above the ascenders; B is simply the less wrong one.

states.name: unfocused
states.gap: The opposite overcorrection: 2 CSS px of air before the caret against 11 CSS px after it, a 5.5:1 lopsided split of the same 16 CSS px gap (A splits it 3.5/9, i.e. 2.6:1). The caret licks the 's' and the space beyond it optically reads as a double space, so 'steps | the' looks mis-spaced every time you stop typing mid-line.
states.gapTheirs: Caret sits off the character grid: its left edge lands ~1 CSS px past the cell boundary after 'steps', leaving 3.5 CSS px of air between the final 's' and the bar (B: 2 CSS px). It reads as parked in the word-space rather than at the insertion point. It is also the taller of the two — 76 device px vs 74, overshooting 11 CSS px above the 't' ascender vs B's 10.
states.verdict: These are the same caret with a 2px shove — 3 CSS px wide, #AEE5FB, one full line-box tall in both — so anyone claiming a real difference is selling something. B wins only because its bar lands within half a pixel of the character cell boundary while A's drifts right into the word-space, and because B overshoots the ascender by 10 CSS px instead of 11. Both commit the same larger crime: a caret 2.5x the ascender height (76/30 and 74/30 device px), a pale blue column of leading that announces the line box instead of the letter you are about to type, at 1.29:1 contrast against a #F9F9F9 page while the text sits at ~15:1. Neither feels like a nib; both feel like a leftover highlight, and with no selection rendered in either shot half this dimension is simply unbuilt.
